sousTitre: The complete history of artificial intelligence, from the first machines to today's agents

diapos.sousTitre: The complete history of artificial intelligence, from the first machines to today's agents
diapos.notes: Welcome the class with a question on the board: “Can a machine think?” Do not answer it: the whole lesson keeps coming back to it. Announce the common thread: the dream of intelligent machines is very old, but AI as a science is seventy years old, and its agents only a few years.

points: Why AI, and why now? (2026)
What is AI? (definitions)
The dream of machines (from Antiquity to 1949)
The birth of AI (1950–1980)
From rules to data (1980–2005)
The deep learning revolution (2006–2017)
Transformers and generative AI (2017–2026)
How does a machine learn? (episode 3: the neural network)
How does a machine read a text? (from words to numbers)
The age of agents (2023–2026)
Summary (from 1206 to 2026)
diapos.notes: This lesson follows Ahmed El-Ghandour's course *The Last Invention*, in the order of its episodes. First, why AI matters today (episode 1), then what it really is. Next, its whole history, without jumping from one period to another: from ancient automata to the models of 2026 (episode 2). Finally, we open the machine: how a neural network learns (episode 3), how a machine reads a text, how an agent acts, before the summary. Tell the students where you are going: we start from today's questions, travel back in time, then return to the present having understood “the magician's trick”. Tip: ask everyone to write down one key date per part; at the end, the class will rebuild the timeline together. Source: Ahmed El-Ghandour's course *The Last Invention* (2026), episodes 1 to 3.

diapos.texte: Every time we think we have understood AI, it surprises us again. Why is everything speeding up now?
diapos.notes: Part one, taken from episode 1 of the course *The Last Invention*. Before the history and before the technology, we look at the present: why has AI become, in just a few years, a matter of states, money, jobs and power? Here is the path of this part: a machine that keeps surprising us, adoption figures never seen before, a race between nations, “thinking factories”, the battle over chips and data, then what AI changes for beginners and for those who make decisions. Tip: open with a quick round: “Which AI tool did you use this week, and what for?” Write three answers on the board: you will come back to them at the end of the part. Source: episode 1 of Ahmed El-Ghandour's *The Last Invention* (2026).

points: It calculated, played chess, translated, wrote, drew, filmed… and tomorrow?
Each time we say “this is its limit”, and each time it goes further
What I thought only a human could do, a machine now does, thousands of times faster
The question of this course: what is AI, and why now?
diapos.notes: The course opens like this: every time we thought we had understood AI, we discovered we were only at the beginning. Again and again, it wakes us up with a new surprise. First the machine calculated (ENIAC, 1946). Then it played chess and beat the world champion (Deep Blue, 1997). Then it translated whole sentences at a time (Google Translate, 2016), wrote texts (GPT-3, 2020), drew pictures (DALL-E, 2021), made videos (Sora, 2024). Tomorrow, perhaps, whole films. At every step we say: “This time it has reached its limit, it won't surprise us again.” And it goes further. The most unsettling part: what I thought made me special as a human, a machine now does, sometimes thousands of times faster. Hence the question of the course: what is AI, and why now? Tip: ask for a show of hands: who has already used an AI to translate? to write? to create an image? Each raised hand is one step of the staircase. Source: episode 1 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); milestones: ENIAC, IBM, Google, OpenAI.

points: In three years, generative AI spread faster than the PC, the mobile phone and the Internet
ChatGPT alone: 900 million users every week (February 2026)
88% of organizations use it in at least one business function (McKinsey, 2025)
2025: $345 billion invested; 2026: over $1 trillion spent on data centers
diapos.notes: The course begins with dizzying figures: in three years, generative AI supposedly reached half of humanity, about 4 billion people. Careful: that figure is not confirmed anywhere. Stanford's report (AI Index 2026) says generative AI reached 53% adoption within three years, faster than the personal computer and the Internet. But Microsoft counts only 18.8% of the world's working-age population (June 2026). ChatGPT alone announced 900 million weekly users in February 2026. In business, 88% of the organizations surveyed by McKinsey use AI. And the money follows: the course says 300 billion; Stanford counts $345 billion of private investment in 2025. For 2026, the firm Dell'Oro expects more than $1 trillion of spending on data centers. Tip: show that two serious sources give different figures, then ask why: who is being counted, and how? Source: episode 1 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Stanford HAI, AI Index 2026; Microsoft, AI Diffusion Report (2026); OpenAI (2026); McKinsey, The State of AI (2025); Dell'Oro Group (2026).

diapos.texte: The first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.
diapos.notes: I. J. Good, a statistician, had worked with Alan Turing at Bletchley Park during the war. The idea of the “last invention” comes from him: a machine able to improve itself would invent everything else. Note the condition, often forgotten: “provided it stays under control”. Two-minute debate: is this science or science fiction?

points: Nations are racing: whoever wins could lead the world in the years to come
“A new nuclear bomb” that does not only destroy: it builds and plans
An economic bet: AI becomes infrastructure, like electricity or the Internet
Investors want to buy the “land” early, before its price soars
diapos.notes: The course puts it with a strong image: AI is, figuratively, the new nuclear bomb. But a bomb that does not only destroy: it gives life, builds, thinks and plans. Every country is racing, because whoever wins could lead the world. This is no exaggeration: on 1 September 2017, Vladimir Putin said that “the one who becomes the leader in this sphere will be the ruler of the world”, and in July 2017 China set itself the goal of becoming the world's primary AI innovation center by 2030. Everyone wants to be first to reach Good's “last invention”, the one that would improve itself. So this is not about cute apps, but an economic bet: AI would become infrastructure, like electricity or the Internet. The course mentions the grandfather who did not buy land when it cost almost nothing: no investor wants to be that grandfather. Tip: ask which other inventions became infrastructure (railways, electricity, the Internet) and what they changed. Source: episode 1 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); V. Putin, 1 September 2017 (CNN); China's New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan, July 2017.

points: The “cloud” is on the ground: buildings full of chips, cables and cooling
The largest AI campuses exceed 1 gigawatt; Meta's Hyperion (Louisiana) aims for 5
5 GW: nearly a quarter of Algeria's record peak demand (almost 22 GW, summer 2026)
Thinking becomes a commodity: produced, sold and billed
diapos.notes: We talk about “the cloud” as if AI floated in the sky. The course corrects this: it is a smart cloud built on solid ground. Inside: chips, miles of cables, cooling machines and a huge electricity bill. The course claims that some data centers burn 30 gigawatts, as much as New York State on a heatwave afternoon. That is an exaggeration for a single site: New York State's record peak is 34 GW (2013), while the largest AI campuses barely exceed 1 GW, like OpenAI's Stargate in Abilene, Texas (1.2 GW). Hyperion, Meta's giant project in Louisiana, aims for 5 GW. In total, according to the International Energy Agency, data centers used 1.5% of the world's electricity in 2024, and this could double by 2030. Hence the course's conclusion: thinking becomes a commodity. Tip: ask how many homes 1 GW can power (800,000 to 1 million American homes, according to New York's grid operator). Source: episode 1 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); NYISO; IEA, Energy and AI (2025); Sonelgaz (August 2026).

diapos.titre: Chips, rare earths, data: the geopolitics of AI
points: October 2022: Washington restricts sales of the most powerful AI chips to China
Beijing answers with metals: gallium and germanium (2023), rare earths (2025)
Every country wonders: American or Chinese models? Where does my data go?
Sovereignty: Saudi Arabia and Algeria (law 18-07) regulate data leaving the country
diapos.notes: Everyone wants to keep what they have. Since 7 October 2022, the United States has banned sales of the most advanced AI chips to China, NVIDIA's first among them; the rules were tightened in 2023 and 2024. China answers, the course says: “You won't sell me your chips? Then I won't sell you my rare metals”, which are essential to make them: licenses became mandatory for gallium and germanium in August 2023, and for seven rare earths in April 2025. These rules keep moving: Washington allowed some sales again in January 2026. Other countries worry: in a conflict, can I depend on the models and servers of one of them? Because data is the fuel of AI. Hence data sovereignty laws: Saudi Arabia (personal data law, 2023) strictly regulates transfers abroad; in Algeria, law 18-07 (2018, amended in 2025) places them under the control of the national data protection authority. Tip: ask students in which country the questions they ask a chatbot are stored. Source: episode 1 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); US Bureau of Industry and Security; China's Ministry of Commerce; Saudi PDPL; Algerian laws 18-07 and 25-11.

points: The industrial revolution took one or two centuries; AI changes society in 3 or 4 years
US software developers aged 22–25: nearly 20% fewer jobs since late 2022
AI does not yet replace the expert: it takes the tasks that train beginners
No apprentice in the workshop today, no master tomorrow
diapos.notes: Every great invention changes society. The industrial revolution moved us from fields to factories: peasants left for the cities, some families grew rich, others lost everything. But it took one to two centuries. We are watching the world change in three or four years. The course's example: programming. A few years ago it was a star job, in high demand and well paid. Today, in the United States, employment of software developers aged 22 to 25 has fallen by nearly 20% from its late-2022 peak, while employment of older developers stayed stable or kept growing (Stanford, 2025). AI is not the only cause, but look at the ladder: AI cannot yet do the expert's work; it does the simple tasks that used to turn beginners into experts. If there is no apprentice in the workshop, who will become the master? Tip: ask your students which tasks of a beginning translator AI already does, and how they can keep learning anyway. Source: episode 1 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); E. Brynjolfsson et al., “Canaries in the Coal Mine?”, Stanford Digital Economy Lab, August 2025.

diapos.titre: The real question: who gives the machine power?
points: It helps decide a loan, a stock purchase, policies for millions of people
It is used in war too… the same kind of model that does your math homework!
The question is no longer “is it intelligent?”
But: who gave it authority? Who tested it? Who answers when it gets it wrong?
diapos.notes: AI does not stop at jobs: it is everywhere, from schools to banks and hospitals. Imagine: you ask for a loan, and an algorithm decides whether you deserve it. On the stock market, it says what to buy and what to sell. In government, it helps make decisions that affect millions of people. And in war: in February 2024, the US military confirmed that Project Maven algorithms had helped it choose targets in Iraq and Syria. In July 2025, the Pentagon signed contracts with OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and xAI, the very companies whose chatbots do your math homework, and that you ask what to do about a pimple on your face! So the question changes: who gave it this power, who tested it, who will be held accountable when it gets it wrong? The European Union (AI Act, 2024) classifies AI credit scoring as “high-risk”: testing and human oversight are mandatory. Tip: five-minute debate: in your future job, which decision would you refuse to entrust to an AI? Source: episode 1 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Bloomberg, 26 February 2024; CDAO (Pentagon), July 2025; Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Annex III.

points: Not “good or bad?”, but: what it does well or badly, for whom, at whose expense
Understanding puts everything in its place: fear or wonder, when each is due
Knowing the trick takes nothing from the magician: we see how skillful he is
The path: its history, then inside the machine (networks, weights, attention)
diapos.notes: End of episode 1. The course does not want to teach you sixty tools: they change too fast. It wants to tell what is happening now, and what led to it. Here is our path: define AI, go through its history in order, then open the machine (neurons, weights, attention) to understand how it sees, reads, speaks and acts. We will not ask whether it is good or bad, but what it does well, what it does badly, who benefits and at whose expense. Because this is not only the story of a machine learning from humans; it is also the story of humans learning from the machine, sometimes fearing it, sometimes growing so attached that they love it. Understanding puts everything in its place: fear when fear is needed, wonder when wonder is needed. The magician stays skillful even when we know his trick; in fact, knowing it is how we measure his skill. Tip: ask everyone to write on a slip of paper the question they would like answered by the end of the course; read them again in the last session. Source: episode 1 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).

diapos.texte: Before telling the story, let us agree on the words: what does “artificial intelligence” mean?
diapos.notes: We now know why AI matters today. Before telling its story, we need to agree on the words. Ahmed El-Ghandour asks the question plainly: if someone asks you “what is AI?”, what do you answer? Many students use ChatGPT every day, but few can define it. This part gives three tools: a definition (a machine that imitates intelligence), three levels (narrow, general, super) and three layers (data, compute, algorithms). They will be our glasses for reading the whole history that follows. Activity: ask three or four students to give their own definition of AI in one sentence; write the key words in a corner of the board and come back to them at the end of this part to see what has changed. Source: Ahmed El-Ghandour's course *The Last Invention* (2026), episode 3, and the teacher's NotebookLM decks.

diapos.titre: And you, what do you call “intelligence”?
points: Understanding a sentence, translating a poem
Recognizing one face among a thousand
Winning at chess, solving a problem
Learning from one's mistakes
Acting alone to reach a goal
diapos.notes: Two minutes of voting by show of hands: which of these abilities does a machine already have? The answer at the end of the lesson: all of them, to varying degrees, but no machine combines them as a human does. The last line, acting alone to reach a goal, defines the agent: it is where the lesson is heading.

points: A simple definition: AI is a machine's attempt to *simulate* intelligence
It does not need to understand: it only needs to *seem* to understand
“Artificial” as in “an artificial smile”: imitated, not just manufactured
“I understand you,” says the chatbot: probably not, but it often helps
diapos.notes: The course starts from a very simple definition: AI is a machine's attempt to *simulate* intelligence. We do not ask it to be intelligent or to understand; we ask it to look as if it does. Hence the word “artificial”. In Arabic the nuance is striking: AI is called «اصطناعي», from the same family as «مُصطنَع» (feigned, like a forced smile), not «صناعي», made in a factory. In English, “artificial” shares its Latin root with “artifice”: skill, but also trickery. Think of artificial flowers: they look real, they decorate the room, but they do not grow. When a chatbot tells you “I understand you” and acts as if it did, does it understand? Probably not. But the imitation is useful: by trying to look intelligent, the machine often gives real help. For literature students: this is Aristotle's *mimesis*, which the Arabic poetics of Avicenna and Averroes calls «المحاكاة», imitation. Question: what other “artificial” thing imitates without being? Source: Ahmed El-Ghandour's course *The Last Invention* (2026), episode 3; etymology: Merriam-Webster (“artifice”).

points: Narrow AI: a genius at one task (Google Maps, chess, video games); it exists
Google Translate: nearly 250 languages… but it cannot play chess
General AI: translating, playing, finding the way… like a human; still theoretical
Superintelligence: far beyond us, perhaps self-aware, with its own goals; unknown
diapos.notes: The course sorts AI into three levels according to what it can do. Narrow AI is designed for a single problem, and it excels at it. Google Translate, which turned 20 in April 2026 and has so often got us out of trouble, is a genius at translation; but it cannot play chess or write code, things that you can do. General AI would be like you: it could translate, play, and find its way through traffic. Ask it for directions: instead of saying “turn right” at once, it would think and ask you “the shortest road or the nicest one?”. Why not always prefer it? Because it can make mistakes, and a narrow model trained on specialized data is often more reliable. Finally, superintelligence: a mind far stronger than ours, perhaps self-aware, able to set its own goals; I. J. Good's “last invention”. Rest assured: we do not even have general AI yet. Question: which narrow AI have you used today? Source: Ahmed El-Ghandour's course *The Last Invention* (2026), episode 3; Google's blog (April 2026).

points: It translates, writes, codes, makes images… and even poems, not always good ones
But it learned from the data it was given, not from the world, and struggles to go further
Narrow or general? Experts disagree; general AI does not exist yet
Money, chips, electricity, algorithms: many think we will get there; let us be ready
diapos.notes: ChatGPT, launched at the end of 2022 and used every week by 900 million people in early 2026, confuses many people: is it narrow or general AI? It has a “general” side: it translates, writes, helps with code, makes images; it even writes poems, sometimes bad ones, but it writes them. Yet a true general AI would learn by trying the world for itself. ChatGPT learned from the data it was given, and it struggles to go beyond it. Experts disagree: in 2025, Demis Hassabis (Google DeepMind) predicted human-level AI within five to ten years, while Yann LeCun argued that we will not get there just by scaling up language models. But with money, chips, electricity and algorithms, the race is on: let us be ready. To get closer to general AI, we will do what we have always done: copy nature, in this case the brain. Activity: ask ChatGPT for a poem in the style of a poet studied in class, then let the class critique it. Source: Ahmed El-Ghandour's course *The Last Invention* (2026), episode 3; OpenAI (February 2026); CNBC (March 2025); *Big Technology* podcast (May 2025).

diapos.titre: What is an AI made of? Three layers
points: Data, the fuel: the texts, images and sounds the machine learns from
Compute, the power: graphics chips (GPUs), servers, data centers
Algorithms, the engine: the recipe that turns data into know-how
The three advance together: the history that follows is the story of these three layers
diapos.notes: Remember part 1: AI is not a cute little app, it is infrastructure. But what is it made of? The NotebookLM decks draw it as three floors. At the bottom, data: the fuel, without which nothing moves. In the middle, compute: thousands of chips working at the same time. At the top, algorithms: the engine, the method that learns. A real example: training Llama 3.1 (Meta, July 2024) took more than 15 trillion word pieces, more than 16,000 NVIDIA H100 chips for several months, and a recipe published in 2017, the Transformer. The key idea: the three layers advance together, and when one is missing, everything stops. You will see that the idea of neural networks, born with the perceptron (1958), only triumphed in 2012, when data and compute had finally caught up with it. On the board: draw a kitchen, with the recipe (algorithm), the ingredients (data) and the fire (compute). What happens if one is missing? Source: Ahmed El-Ghandour's course *The Last Invention* (2026), episode 1, and the teacher's NotebookLM decks; Meta AI (July 2024).

diapos.texte: Long before computers, humans imagined and built machines that imitate life, then machines that calculate.
diapos.notes: First stage: AI did not come from nowhere. Two lines meet here: automata, which imitate movement, and calculating machines, which imitate reasoning.

points: Greek myth: Talos, a bronze giant who guards Crete
1st century: Hero of Alexandria describes theater automata
1739: Vaucanson's duck flaps its wings and “digests”
Around 1770: the Jaquet-Droz Writer traces letters with a quill
diapos.notes: An automaton reproduces a movement set in advance by its gears or cams. It decides nothing: that is the difference from an AI. Ask: does the Jaquet-Droz Writer really “write”?

diapos.titre: Al-Jazari, the engineer of ingenious machines
points: Engineer at the Artuqid court, in Upper Mesopotamia
In 1206, writes *The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices*
Describes some fifty machines: clocks, pumps, automata
His elephant clock marks the hours with automata
diapos.notes: Al-Jazari shows that the tradition of automata runs through the medieval Arab and Muslim world. His detailed drawings still make it possible to rebuild his machines today. Be careful: these are automata programmed in advance, not machines that learn.

points: 1642: Blaise Pascal builds the Pascaline, which adds
1673: Leibniz presents a machine that multiplies
1837: Charles Babbage designs the Analytical Engine, programmable with punched cards
The Analytical Engine would never be completed in his lifetime
diapos.notes: A key transition: a machine that calculates takes over part of the work of the mind. Babbage's Analytical Engine already has a memory and a calculating unit, like our computers.

points: 1843: her notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine
In them, she writes an algorithm to compute Bernoulli numbers
She imagines that the machine could compose music
diapos.citation: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything.
diapos.notes: Her sentence, “Lady Lovelace's objection”, would be discussed by Turing a century later: does a machine only do what it is told? A question for the class: does a model that writes a poem create something?

points: 1854: George Boole reduces reasoning to calculations on true and false
1936: Alan Turing describes an abstract machine capable of any calculation
A tape, a read head, a table of rules: the “Turing machine”
Every computer today is, in principle, a Turing machine
diapos.notes: Boole provides the alphabet (true, false, and, or, not); Turing provides the universal machine. Show the animation: the head reads a cell, writes, moves, changes state. With rules this simple, anything can be calculated.

diapos.role: Mathematician, father of theoretical computer science
points: 1936: the universal machine
1939–1945: helps break the Enigma code at Bletchley Park
1950: “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, the founding paper
diapos.citation: I propose to consider the question, ‘Can machines think?’
diapos.notes: Turing replaces an impossible question (“think”) with an observable test, the imitation game. This is the founding move of AI. The quoted sentence opens his 1950 paper.

points: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts model a neuron as a calculation
It adds up input signals and “fires” above a threshold
It is the ancestor of all today's neural networks
diapos.notes: The first bridge between biology and calculation. Draw on the board: three inputs, weights, a sum, a threshold. We will find exactly this diagram again with the perceptron in 1958, then in deep learning.

points: 1945: ENIAC, 30 tonnes, calculates ballistic trajectories
1948: Claude Shannon founds information theory
The bit becomes the unit of all information: text, image, sound
The machines finally exist; now they must be made “intelligent”
diapos.notes: ENIAC fills an entire room and is programmed by plugging in cables. Shannon, for his part, would be one of the four signatories of the Dartmouth proposal. End of the first stage: everything is ready for the birth of AI.

diapos.texte: A question that seemed absurd: can a computer think? Two answers will compete: write rules, or copy neurons.
diapos.notes: Where does the real history of AI begin? In the middle of the twentieth century. In 1950 the English mathematician Alan Turing, the man of the imitation game, asked a question that seemed almost ridiculous at the time: “Can machines think?” Picture it: back then a computer filled a whole room and did nothing but calculate. Yet these strange ideas, more than 75 years old, became the foundation of everything that followed. This part tells a thirty-year adventure: the age of rules (“if… then…”), then a young researcher who preferred to copy the brain's neurons, the excitement of the press and, in the end, the fall: the first AI winter. Remember the two paths, rules or neurons: the rest of the story is their rivalry. Tip: write “Can a computer think?” on the board and let the class vote (yes, no, it depends); vote again at the end of the part. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); A. M. Turing, “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, *Mind*, 1950.

points: A judge converses in writing with two hidden interlocutors
One is a human, the other a machine
If the judge cannot tell them apart, the machine “passes”
diapos.notes: Act out the scene: two hidden volunteers, a judge, five minutes of written questions. Discussion: does the test measure intelligence, or the art of creating an illusion? Today's chatbots have revived this debate.

diapos.texte: Every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.
diapos.auteur: J. McCarthy, M. Minsky, N. Rochester, C. Shannon
diapos.source: Proposal for the Dartmouth workshop, August 31, 1955
diapos.notes: This is the text in which the expression “artificial intelligence” appears. The hypothesis is very ambitious: everything intelligence does could be described precisely. Ask: is that true of humor? Of poetic intuition?

diapos.role: Computer scientist who gave AI its name
points: Summer 1956: organizes the Dartmouth workshop, the birth certificate of AI
1958: creates the Lisp language, long the language of AI
With him: Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, Nathaniel Rochester
diapos.notes: The Dartmouth workshop brought together about ten researchers during the summer of 1956. It produced no major discovery, but it gave the discipline a name, a community and a program.

points: The Logic Theorist by Allen Newell, Herbert Simon and Cliff Shaw
It proves 38 of the first 52 theorems of *Principia Mathematica*
For one of them, a more elegant proof than the authors' own
A key idea: searching among possibilities with rules
diapos.notes: The Logic Theorist embodies symbolic AI: symbols, rules, a search through a tree of possibilities. It is the same logic as forward chaining in the chapter 3 tutorial (TD).

diapos.titre: The age of rules: IF… THEN…
points: The first era of AI: the age of logic, or of rules
To act like us, the machine is given rules: “IF this, THEN that”
The result: a good executor that follows steps, not an intelligence
But rules are made to be broken… and a young researcher is about to do it
diapos.notes: After Turing and Dartmouth comes the first great era of AI: the age of logic, known as *rule-based* AI. The idea is simple: if we want the machine to behave like an intelligent human, let us give it logical rules, and it will follow them. “Dear Machine, if this happens, you will do that.” The Logic Theorist we have just seen worked this way. The problem, says Ahmed El-Ghandour, is that this does not produce intelligence: it produces a good executor, someone who follows steps without understanding. And rules, as the saying goes, are made to be broken: that is exactly what a young researcher will do in 1957. Tip: give the students two minutes to write the IF… THEN… rules that recognise a sonnet (fourteen lines, a fixed rhyme scheme), then the rules that recognise “a beautiful poem”. Why is the second list impossible? Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).

diapos.nom: Frank Rosenblatt and the Mark I Perceptron
diapos.role: Psychologist at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory (Buffalo, USA)
points: Instead of fixed rules, learn as a human does: copy the neurons of the brain
A “retina” of 20 × 20 = 400 photocells turns the image into numbers
Circle or square? When it is wrong, it corrects its weights: it learns from its mistakes
diapos.citation: The first machine which is capable of having an original idea
diapos.notes: 1957, in an aeronautical research laboratory linked to Cornell University, in Buffalo. A young psychologist, Frank Rosenblatt, decides to break the rules. Instead of making the machine follow fixed rules, he wants it to learn the way we do. He looks at the brain: nerve cells receive signals, process them and send one out in turn. His idea: do not invent intelligence, copy nature's. He first simulates his “perceptron” on an IBM 704 computer, then builds a real machine, the Mark I, shown to the public on 23 June 1960: a camera with 400 photocells, and weights set by knobs that small electric motors turn by themselves. It is shown a shape: circle or square? If it is wrong, it corrects its weights to answer better next time. Judge, make a mistake, correct yourself: very simple, and immense. Tip: show the photo and ask the class where the machine's “eye”, “neurons” and “memory” are. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention*; Smithsonian, Mark I Perceptron record; Cornell Chronicle, 2019.

points: Each input is multiplied by a *weight*, then everything is added up
Sum above the threshold → 1, below → 0: like a neuron that fires or not
An engineer? The baccalaureate grade weighs a lot; height, almost nothing
An athlete? The reverse: height counts (volleyball, basketball). Each clue has its weight
diapos.notes: Here is how the perceptron “thinks”, with Ahmed El-Ghandour's example. The machine receives input information. It multiplies each piece by a weight, adds everything up and compares the total with a number fixed in advance, the threshold. Above the threshold, it answers 1; below, 0. That is what a neuron in the brain does: it sends a signal, or it does not. Why weights? Because not all information is equal. To guess whether the person in front of me is an engineer, their baccalaureate grade matters a lot; their height, 1.75 m, tells me nothing. To guess whether they are an athlete, it is the reverse: the grade matters little, but if the person is very tall, they may play volleyball or basketball. For the perceptron, learning means finding the right weights. Tip: have the class guess a volunteer's job from two clues written on the board, and ask which clue “weighs” more; weights come back in detail in part 8. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention*; F. Rosenblatt, *Psychological Review*, 1958.

diapos.texte: The Navy revealed the embryo of an electronic computer today that it expects will be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence.
diapos.source: “New Navy Device Learns by Doing”, July 8, 1958
diapos.notes: July 7, 1958, in Washington. The US Navy, which funds Rosenblatt's work, invites the press. In front of the reporters, a huge IBM 704 computer is fed punched cards; after about fifty trials, it learns to tell cards marked on the left from cards marked on the right. That is all. But the next day, the *New York Times* announces a machine that will walk, talk and be conscious of itself. As episode 2 tells it, the press gets carried away: “Watch out, make way, a revolution is coming!” And the US government opens the taps. This is the height of the Cold War: after the Soviet Sputnik (October 1957), Washington created ARPA in February 1958, an agency meant to keep the country ahead in technology. A machine that learns could serve the military; people believe intelligence is almost solved. Tip: put side by side what the machine really did (left or right?) and what the newspaper wrote; ask the students to spot the verbs that exaggerate. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention*; *The New York Times*, July 8, 1958; Cornell Chronicle, 2019.

points: At IBM, Arthur Samuel writes a checkers program that improves by playing against itself
1959: his paper launches the term “machine learning”
After 8 to 10 hours of play, the program plays better than its own creator
Two paths emerge: writing the rules, or having them learned
diapos.notes: Meanwhile, at IBM, an engineer takes another road towards learning. Arthur Samuel does not copy neurons: he writes a checkers program that remembers positions it has already seen and plays against itself, keeping what leads to victory. On 24 February 1956, the program appears on television; IBM's head, Thomas Watson, had predicted that the demonstration would lift the company's share price by 15 points, and it did. In 1959, Samuel publishes a paper that opens like this: a computer can be programmed so that it will learn to play a better game of checkers than can be played by the person who wrote the program. The often-quoted definition, “learning without being explicitly programmed”, sums up his idea well, but it is not in the paper. Tip: ask the students what “learning” means: memorising, practising, understanding? Which of these does Samuel's machine do? Source: A. L. Samuel, *IBM Journal of Research and Development*, July 1959; University of Alberta, “Arthur Samuel's Legacy”.

diapos.texte: Machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work a man can do.
diapos.notes: The promises of the time were excessive. Twenty years later, in 1985, the field was very far from them. Ask students to find a current promise about AI and to consider how it will be judged in twenty years.

echanges.texte: They're always bugging us about something or other.
CAN YOU THINK OF A SPECIFIC EXAMPLE
Well, my boyfriend made me come here.
YOUR BOYFRIEND MADE YOU COME HERE

diapos.notes: ELIZA understands nothing: it spots keywords and sends the sentence back using transformation rules. Yet users confided their secrets to it. Weizenbaum was troubled by this all his life. This is the “ELIZA effect”: attributing understanding to a machine that answers well.

diapos.titre: Shakey, the first robot that reasons
points: Built at the Stanford Research Institute (SRI)
It perceives its environment with a camera
It plans a sequence of actions to reach a goal
The A* algorithm, still used to compute routes, was created for it
diapos.notes: Shakey is a direct ancestor of agents: it perceives, plans, acts. But it takes minutes to decide to push a box. Remember the pattern perceive, plan, act: it comes back at the end of the lesson.

points: 1969: Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert (MIT) publish the book *Perceptrons*
The perceptron splits two groups with one straight line: circle or square, sick or healthy
The two-key door: it opens if one OR the other turns a key, but not if both do
It needs a rule on top of a rule: no line is enough. This is “exclusive OR” (XOR)
diapos.notes: While the press dreams, two MIT researchers take a close look at the machine. Marvin Minsky, one of the fathers of AI at Dartmouth, has known Rosenblatt since high school in New York, and the two men have already clashed in public. In 1969, with the mathematician Seymour Papert, he publishes *Perceptrons*. The message: this perceptron the newspapers talk about is very simple; like a small child who says “daddy” or “mummy”, it separates two groups with a line. The episode explains it with a door: you are outside, your spouse inside, each with a key. The door opens if one of you turns a key; it stays shut if nobody does… and also if you both turn at the same moment. You need a rule on top of a rule. Several layers of neurons could do it, but nobody yet knows how to train them, and Minsky and Papert sense that this path is “sterile”. Tip: have two students act out the door and let the class guess the rule. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention*; M. Minsky and S. Papert, *Perceptrons*, MIT Press, 1969.

points: After *Perceptrons*, fear: the money for neural networks stops
1973: the Lighthill report (United Kingdom) finds the promises unkept, and funding is cut
Around 1974, in the United States, DARPA demands military results and cuts its funding
Neural networks: some fifteen years of doubt, “only the brain is intelligent”
diapos.notes: After Minsky and Papert's book, says Ahmed El-Ghandour, people became very afraid. The enthusiasm fell, the money stopped, and the pause was not short: for neural networks, it lasted about fifteen years. People told themselves: we fooled ourselves, we are searching in a void; intelligence is the brain, and only the brain holds its secret. Other promises disappointed too. In 1973, the mathematician James Lighthill handed the British government a harsh report: nowhere had the discoveries had the promised impact, and as soon as a problem grows, the number of possibilities to examine explodes. Most British universities lost their AI funding. In the United States, DARPA (formerly ARPA), which since 1969 could only fund research useful to the military, cut its funding in turn. This was the first AI winter. Rosenblatt would not see the spring: he died in 1971, on his 43rd birthday, in a boating accident. Tip: draw the curve of expectations on the board and place on it 1958 (the *New York Times*) and 1973 (Lighthill). Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention*; J. Lighthill, *Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey*, 1973.

diapos.texte: Rules conquer companies, then run into reality. Meanwhile, machines start learning from examples.
diapos.notes: We are coming out of the first winter. In the 1980s, AI comes back through the door of business: experts' knowledge is turned into IF… THEN… rules, and expert systems sell well. But the real world is full of exceptions, and the rules end up cracking. Meanwhile, another idea grows quietly: instead of writing everything down, show the machine examples and let it learn, like a child. The course calls this AI's spring, brought by a revolution: machine learning. This part runs from 1980 to 2005: rules, the return of neural networks, AI's first real job, a second winter, and a chess match that made headlines around the world. Tip: draw two columns on the board, “rules” and “examples”; at each slide, ask the students which column it belongs in. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).

points: A fact base, a base of IF … THEN … rules, an inference engine
1970s: MYCIN, at Stanford, diagnoses blood infections
1980: XCON configures computers for the company DEC
Companies invest: AI becomes an industry
diapos.notes: Link this to session 6: the role play on poetic forms is a small expert system. MYCIN had about 600 rules written with doctors.

points: Cat, dog or hyena? All have a tail, two eyes and fur: rules get lost
It must learn like a child: see many examples and spot the differences
1980s: faster, cheaper computers; researchers can experiment freely
Data is AI's gym: the more data, the stronger the muscle
diapos.notes: The course suggests a small experiment. Imagine a program that recognizes animals: you show it a photo, and it answers “cat”, “dog” or “hyena”. With rules, it is almost impossible. “A cat has a tail”? So do the dog and the hyena. Two eyes, fur: everything is shared. We need another method: not only writing rules, but letting the machine learn, like a child who looks at the world and discovers the differences little by little. The timing is right: in the 1980s, computers become more powerful and cheaper, and researchers no longer wait for state funding to try things out. Universities also share data: in 1987, the University of California, Irvine opens a public library of datasets that is still used today. Data is AI's gym: the more it trains, the better it spots what repeats. Practice makes perfect. Tip: ask the students to write a rule that tells a cat from a dog, then look for the counterexample together. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); UCI Machine Learning Repository (1987).

diapos.titre: Two ways to build an AI

points: An expert writes the rules
Explainable: the reasoning can be followed
Brittle outside its domain
Example: an expert system
The machine draws patterns from examples
Often hard to explain
Robust, if there is plenty of data
Example: a spam filter

diapos.notes: Have students classify three objects: a spellchecker, a machine translator, a GPS. Today, the best systems often combine both approaches.

points: The idea: stack perceptrons in layers, like the layers of a lasagna
Each layer checks one condition and passes on to the next: XOR becomes possible
The harder the problem, the more layers you add
1986: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularize backpropagation to train them
diapos.notes: After the winter, some researchers say: we want an AI that resembles human intelligence, so let's really imitate the brain, with an artificial neural network. The perceptron's flaw was that it applied a single rule, a single straight line. The solution: several layers of perceptrons, one on top of the other. The course uses the image of a baked dish, lasagna or béchamel: each layer receives the work of the one before. First condition met? Great, on to the second, then the third… The harder the problem, the taller the dish, and XOR is no longer a wall. What remained was how to train all these layers. In October 1986, David Rumelhart, a psychologist (in the photo, in 1991), Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams publish the method in the journal Nature. The mathematical idea had existed since the 1970s; they make it clear, convincing and famous. Tip: ask what happens to the lasagna if one layer goes wrong: the whole dish suffers, so we must find the faulty layer (next slide). Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, Nature, vol. 323 (9 October 1986).

points: The machine answers; the teacher compares with the right answer: right or wrong?
If wrong, it goes back through the layers: which weights caused the error, and by how much?
It corrects those weights and tries again, thousands of times: this is backpropagation
A teacher who knows the answer: this is *supervised* learning
diapos.notes: The course explains the 1986 idea very simply. The computer receives an input and gives an output. But when it is told it was wrong, it goes back: which weights made me wrong, and each by how much? It changes them a little and tries again. Right? Great. Wrong? It starts over. At this stage, the machine learns like a small child: “What digit is this?” “Five.” The teacher corrects: “Well done!” or “No, it's a three.” Humans let the machine learn, but they supervise it: this is supervised learning. And the machine has an advantage: each correction stays written in its weights; no need to cram the night before the exam. Careful: this does not mean it never makes mistakes again; part 8 will show that it can learn too much, or not enough. Tip: act out the scene: one student is the machine, another is the teacher, who gives the right answer after each mistake. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, Nature (1986).

diapos.role: French researcher at Bell Labs, later head of AI research at Meta
points: 1989: his network reads handwritten digits on US zip codes
For the first time, AI does a real job, outside the laboratory
From 1996, LeNet reads checks: by 2001, about 10% of all US checks
diapos.notes: The years go by, and here we are in 1989. An ambitious young Frenchman, Yann LeCun, has worked in Toronto with Geoffrey Hinton and then joined Bell Labs in the United States. He trains a neural network, with backpropagation, to read handwritten digits: “this is a 3; this is a 5.” The US Postal Service provides 9,298 digits taken from zip codes on letters sorted in Buffalo. It sounds simple; it is a feat, because every hand writes in its own way. Above all, for the first time, AI does a useful job outside the laboratory. From 1996, machines built by the company NCR around this network (LeNet) read the handwritten amount on checks; by 2001 they read about 10% of all checks in the United States. The bank clerk no longer has to decipher every digit. Until then, the examples were toys; now the public sees what AI is for. Tip: write a 1 and a 7 “the French way” and then “the American way”: what makes reading hard for a machine? Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); LeCun et al., Neural Computation (1989) and Proceedings of the IEEE (1998).

points: 1987: the Lisp machine market collapses; expert systems disappoint
Networks remain weak: training too slow, computers not powerful enough
Not failure, but inflated expectations: after 5 goals, 2 goals feel like a defeat
For neural networks, the cold lasts until about 2006
diapos.notes: The course puts it well: when something wonderful happens, we start dreaming very big, until we hit the wall of reality. People announced that AI would soon replace humans at everything; the world discovers that it is not moving that fast. On the rules side: in 1987, the market for Lisp machines, special computers for AI, collapses in the face of cheaper workstations and PCs; expert systems are expensive to maintain and fail outside their domain. On the neural side: networks remain imprecise and training them takes a long time. El-Ghandour insists: the cause is not failure, the work was good; the cause is expectations. If your team scores five goals in the first match, two goals in the next one feel like a defeat. Many researchers then avoid the word “AI” and speak of “informatics” or “machine learning”. Tip: ask whether, in 2026, our expectations are not very high too: what is being promised today? Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); D. Crevier, AI: The Tumultuous History of the Search for Artificial Intelligence (1993).

diapos.role: IBM's computer beats the world chess champion
points: New York, six games: 2 wins, 1 loss, 3 draws, so 3½ to 2½
Game 2: a move so “human” that Kasparov accuses IBM of cheating
No neural network: 200 million positions per second and experts' rules
diapos.notes: The second winter is not cold every day: there are a few sunny days, when the rain stops and you feel a little warmth. May 1997, New York. IBM has its supercomputer Deep Blue play Garry Kasparov, world chess champion since 1985. A year earlier, in Philadelphia, Kasparov had won 4 to 2. This time, Kasparov wins the first game, Deep Blue the second, then come three draws; on 11 May, the machine wins the last one: 3½ to 2½. Kasparov cannot believe it. In game 2, the machine played a calm, almost creative, “human” move; he accuses IBM of bringing in a grandmaster. No evidence was ever found; IBM declines a rematch and retires the machine. The surprise: Deep Blue uses no neural network. It calculates very fast, with 480 special chips, and judges positions with rules tuned with grandmasters. Tip: have the class vote, “Is Deep Blue intelligent?”, and keep the result for AlphaGo (part 6). Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); IBM, “Deep Blue” (ibm.com/history); Campbell, Hoane and Hsu, “Deep Blue”, Artificial Intelligence (2002).

evenements.texte: A network learns backgammon by playing against itself, without human games
Hochreiter and Schmidhuber give networks a memory to read sequences
Viola and Jones: a machine learns to spot faces in real time
Filters learn from your own emails to recognize spam
A Stanford driverless car wins DARPA's desert race

diapos.notes: During the second winter, machine learning moves forward quietly. In 1992, TD-Gammon, by Gerald Tesauro (IBM), learns backgammon by playing hundreds of thousands of games against itself, until it comes close to the best players. In 1997, LSTM memory lets networks follow a sentence over time; Google Translate will use it in 2016. In 2001, Paul Viola and Michael Jones train a machine to find faces in an image in real time; their method will end up in digital cameras. In 2002, the programmer Paul Graham proposes spam filters that learn from your own messages. In 2005, Stanley, Stanford University's car, drives 212 km through the desert on its own and wins 2 million dollars. Notice that AI becomes invisible: it sorts mail, reads checks, filters spam, without being called AI. This is the “AI effect”: as soon as a technique works, people stop calling it intelligence. Tip: ask the students to name an “invisible” AI they used today. Source: additions to episode 2 of *The Last Invention*: Tesauro (1995); Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997); Viola and Jones (2001); P. Graham, A Plan for Spam (2002); Thrun et al. (2006).

diapos.texte: In the middle of winter, one researcher revives deep networks. In 2012, data, graphics cards and algorithms come together: the machine learns to see, to create, then to beat the champions.
diapos.notes: Sixth stage, and it is an awakening. In 2006, it is still winter for neural networks: almost nobody believes in them any more. The course then tells a series of dramatic twists. A stubborn researcher, Geoffrey Hinton, shows how to train a network with many layers. NVIDIA turns video game graphics cards into giant calculators. Fei-Fei Li gathers millions of labeled images. In 2011, Watson and Siri take AI out of the lab. In 2012, after Google's cat, AlexNet makes the three gears mesh, and AI enters what the course calls its “second spring”, the one we are still living in. Then come the forger and the detective, and AlphaGo. The word “deep” refers to the number of layers in the network, not to depth of thought. Tip: draw three columns on the board, “algorithms”, “data”, “compute”, and ask the students to put each event of this part in the right column. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).

diapos.role: Researcher at the University of Toronto, pioneer of neural networks
points: He defends neural networks through both winters, against almost everyone
2006: he trains a deep network layer by layer; “deep” means many layers
2018 Turing Award (with Bengio and LeCun), 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics (with Hopfield)
diapos.notes: It is 2006 and, for neural networks, it is still night. Almost everyone thinks that training a deep network is impossible. Remember the lasagna: we stack layers of neurons; the more layers there are, the more you must go up and down to adjust the weights, and the longer the calculation. Geoffrey Hinton, who never gave up, then publishes with Simon Osindero and Yee-Whye Teh a paper with a dry title: “A fast learning algorithm for deep belief nets”. The idea is very simple: instead of training all the layers at once, you train them one by one, layer after layer. His network recognizes handwritten digits better than the best methods of the time. Before this paper, the course says, the world was one thing; after it, another. In 2023, Hinton left Google to speak freely about the risks of AI. Tip: ask “What is deep in deep learning?”; expected answer: the number of layers. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Hinton, Osindero and Teh, Neural Computation, 2006; ACM (2018 Turing Award); NobelPrize.org (Physics 2024).

points: Graphics cards (GPUs) are made for video games: millions of pixels at once
2007: with CUDA, NVIDIA lets researchers program them for any calculation
A CPU has a few big cores; a GPU has hundreds, then thousands, of small ones
A network trains up to 70 times faster; in 2016, Google unveils its TPU chips
diapos.notes: Hinton's paper alone would not have been enough, the course says: machines were needed. In November 2006, NVIDIA, which makes graphics cards for video games, announces CUDA; the tools come out in 2007. A researcher can now use a graphics card as a giant calculator. Why is that so useful? The processor (CPU) is a few very strong math teachers who solve problems one at a time. The graphics card (GPU) is a lecture hall of thousands of pupils who each do one small multiplication, all at the same time. And a neural network is nothing but a mountain of small multiplications: inputs × weights. In 2009, a Stanford team trains a deep network up to 70 times faster on GPUs: weeks of computing become a day. Google goes further: its own AI chips, the TPUs, run from 2015 and are unveiled in 2016; they will power AlphaGo. Tip: one student does ten multiplications alone, ten students do one each: who finishes first? Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); NVIDIA (CUDA announcement, 2006); Raina, Madhavan and Ng, ICML 2009; Google I/O (TPU, May 2016).

diapos.role: Researcher at Princeton, then Stanford: she bets on data
points: 2009: ImageNet; it will grow to over 14 million images in nearly 22,000 categories
Labeled by hand by nearly 49,000 people in 167 countries, via Amazon Mechanical Turk
From 2010 to 2017, a yearly contest: which program best recognizes 1,000 categories?
diapos.notes: While Hinton works on algorithms and NVIDIA on compute, a young researcher takes care of the third gear: data. Fei-Fei Li starts from a simple idea: a child learns to see by looking at thousands of things; the machine also needs its “gym”. Around 2007, at Princeton, she launches a project many find outrageous: gather pictures of almost everything that exists, and name each one. The solution: Amazon Mechanical Turk, a platform where nearly 49,000 workers in 167 countries sort and label the photos, paid per task. In 2009, ImageNet is presented with 3.2 million images; it will grow to more than 14 million. From 2010, a yearly contest pits the best programs against each other on 1,000 categories. In the first two years, progress is slow: 28%, then 26% error… until 2012. Tip: open a debate: who are the invisible workers behind AI, and how are they paid? Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026), for the role of data; Deng et al., CVPR 2009; Russakovsky et al., International Journal of Computer Vision, 2015.

points: February 2011: IBM's Watson beats the two greatest champions of the TV quiz *Jeopardy!*
Clues full of puns: it must grasp the context, not just know facts
Watson wins 1 million dollars, which IBM gives to charity
October 2011: Siri arrives on the iPhone 4S; millions of people talk to their phone
diapos.notes: After Deep Blue, IBM wants to shine on television. Its new program, Watson, takes part in Jeopardy!, a very popular American TV quiz. It is not an ordinary quiz like “What is the capital of Egypt?”: you are given the answer and must find the question, and the clues are full of puns and hints. Understanding language and context: exactly what people said a machine could never do. In the episodes aired from 14 to 16 February 2011, Watson, with no Internet connection, faces Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter and ends with 77,147 dollars, against 24,000 and 21,600. It also makes mistakes: to a clue about American cities, it answers “Toronto”, followed by five question marks. In October, Apple launches Siri on the iPhone 4S; Siri was born at SRI, the institute of the robot Shakey. Tip: ask the course's riddle: a country that starts with “al”, ends with “al”, with a pillar of Islam in the middle (answer: الصومال, Somalia, with صوم, fasting, in the middle). Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); IBM, “Watson, Jeopardy! champion”; Apple, press release of 4 October 2011.

diapos.titre: 2012: the machine discovers the cat on its own
points: Google Brain (Andrew Ng, Jeff Dean) links 1,000 computers: 16,000 processor cores
The network watches 10 million images from YouTube videos; nobody tells it anything
On its own, it forms a “cat” detector: this is *unsupervised* learning
First sign that a deep network can find concepts, not just memorize
diapos.notes: Siri has opened the way; Google does not want to stay behind. Its Google Brain team, with Andrew Ng from Stanford and Jeff Dean, builds a huge neural network: more than a billion connections. For three days, it is shown 10 million images taken from YouTube videos. This time, nobody tells it “this is a cat, this is a human”. It is only told, as the course puts it: “go into the sea and learn to swim by yourself”. Little by little, the shapes that repeat become one thing, and one neuron of the network starts reacting to cat faces, which are everywhere on YouTube. All it lacks is the word “cat”. Jeff Dean told the New York Times: “We never told it during the training, ‘This is a cat.’ It basically invented the concept of a cat.” The machine may not understand, but it seems to. Tip: show three very different cats and ask what they have in common, without saying the word “cat”. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Le, Ranzato et al., ICML 2012; New York Times, June 2012.

points: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton (Toronto) train a deep network on two gaming GPUs
2012 ImageNet contest: 15.3% error, against 26.2% for the runner-up
Algorithms (deep networks) + data (ImageNet) + compute (GPUs): everything meets
AI's second spring begins: the era of deep learning
diapos.notes: Everything is ready: Hinton's algorithm, Fei-Fei Li's images, NVIDIA's graphics cards. In 2012, three Toronto researchers bring them together: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, a future co-founder of OpenAI, and their professor, Geoffrey Hinton. Their network, AlexNet, has 60 million parameters, that is, weights to adjust. It trains for five to six days on two video game graphics cards, in Alex's bedroom at his parents' house. In the ImageNet contest, the machine must say what each photo shows, among 1,000 categories; it gets five guesses, and it counts as an error if the right answer is not among them. AlexNet is wrong 15.3 times out of 100; the runner-up, 26.2 times. As the course says: it did not just win, it crushed the competition. Just one letter's difference, GPU instead of CPU, but years ahead. We no longer stop at one or two layers: we build real towers of lasagna. Tip: ask which gears were missing in 1986, when backpropagation appeared (answer: data and compute). Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, NeurIPS 2012; ILSVRC 2012 results.

diapos.titre: A deep network, layer by layer
points: The first layers detect simple features: edges, blobs
The next layers combine them: shapes, textures, parts
The last ones recognize whole objects: “cat”, “car”
Each layer learns by itself what to detect
diapos.notes: Show the animation: the signal crosses the layers from left to right. It is the same with a text: letters, words, phrases, meaning. Nobody writes down what each neuron should detect: it learns it.

points: Ian Goodfellow invents GANs: two networks that train against each other
The forger makes fake images; the detective tries to expose them
Each time it is caught, the forger improves; so does the detective
Almost real images, then “deepfakes”: AI no longer only judges, it creates
diapos.notes: Until now, AI mostly judges: cat or dog, which digit, which disease. In 2014, a Montreal PhD student, Ian Goodfellow, teaches it to create. One evening, in a Montreal brewpub, Les Trois Brasseurs, friends ask him how to make a computer produce photos. He has an idea: make two networks argue, for the good of both. Back home, he codes it during the night, and it works the first time; the paper even thanks the pub “for stimulating our creativity”. The first network is a forger: it makes fake images. The second is a detective: it must say whether an image is real or fake. Each time it is caught, the forger tries again and does better, and the detective becomes sharper. At the end of the race: faces that do not exist, almost perfect. The downside: in 2017 the word “deepfake” is born, for fake videos of real people. Tip: show a real face and a generated one (for example on thispersondoesnotexist.com) and have the class vote. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Goodfellow et al., “Generative Adversarial Nets”, NeurIPS 2014; MIT Technology Review, “The GANfather”, 2018.

points: A 19 × 19 board, black and white stones: you must surround your opponent
Born in China over 2,500 years ago, it is a game of intuition more than calculation
Chess: about 10⁴³ possible positions (Shannon, 1950); go: about 10¹⁷⁰
That is far more than the roughly 10⁸⁰ atoms in the observable universe
diapos.notes: Episode 2 opens with a game few of us know: go. On a board of 19 lines by 19, one player places black stones, the other white stones; to win, you must surround your opponent, as in a pincer. The winner has always been the one with intuition and flair. In 1950, the mathematician Claude Shannon estimated that chess has about 10⁴³ possible positions, a 1 followed by 43 zeros, and about 10¹²⁰ different games. That is huge, but nothing compared with go: about 10¹⁷⁰ legal positions, according to the exact count published in 2016. Count all the atoms in the observable universe: about 10⁸⁰, far fewer. So brute-force calculation, Deep Blue's weapon at chess, is not enough. The course concludes carefully: as far as we know, it is the most complex game in human history. This is the challenge that DeepMind, a Google company, decides to take on with AlphaGo. Tip: write 10¹⁷⁰ in full on the board and let a student count the zeros. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Shannon, “Programming a Computer for Playing Chess”, 1950; J. Tromp, “The Number of Legal Go Positions”, 2016.

points: Five games against Lee Sedol, a go legend: everyone expects the human to win
Game 2, move 37: a move no human would have played; experts think it is a mistake
AlphaGo wins 4–1; Lee Sedol wins game 4 with a brilliant move of his own, move 78
diapos.citation: It's not a human move. I've never seen a human play this move. So beautiful.
diapos.source: Fan Hui, European go champion, in *Wired*, March 2016
diapos.notes: This is the story that opens episode 2. March 2016, Seoul. On one side, Lee Sedol, a go legend with eighteen world titles; on the other, AlphaGo, DeepMind's program. Everyone expects the human to win: go needs intuition. Game 1: the machine wins. “Beginner's luck”, the audience thinks. Game 2: on move 37, AlphaGo places a stone so strange that the commentators think it is a mistake; by its own estimate, a human would have played it only once in 10,000 times. Lee Sedol leaves the room for a moment, then takes nearly 15 minutes to reply. This is no longer calculation, the course says: it is creation. Game 3: lost again. In game 4, Lee Sedol finds a brilliant move of his own, move 78, and wins. Game 5 is lost: 4–1. In 2019, Lee Sedol retired: AI is, he said, “an entity that cannot be defeated”. Tip: repeat the Deep Blue vote: is AlphaGo intelligent? Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026), which wrongly places move 37 in game 3; Silver et al., Nature, 2016; Wired, March 2016.

diapos.titre: AlphaZero, then AlphaFold: from games to science
points: 2017: AlphaGo Zero learns go by playing against itself, without a single human game
After 3 days, it wins 100–0 against the version that beat Lee Sedol
AlphaZero also learns chess and shogi, from the rules alone, in a few hours
2020: AlphaFold predicts protein shapes; 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Hassabis, Jumper)
diapos.notes: As the course says: the story does not end in Seoul, it begins there. AlphaGo had first studied 30 million positions from human games, then played against itself. In 2017, DeepMind removes the human teachers: AlphaGo Zero is given only the rules of go. It plays against itself, makes mistakes, tries again: this is reinforcement learning, which we will see in part 8. After three days, it wins 100–0 against the version that beat Lee Sedol. Then AlphaZero learns other games from their rules alone: in four hours, it overtakes Stockfish, the champion chess program. Finally, the course says, they think: enough playing, let's move on to biology. In 2020, AlphaFold predicts the three-dimensional shape of proteins, a fifty-year-old challenge. In 2024, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, with David Baker. The course's lesson: AI starts small, almost trivial, then grows and spreads. Tip: ask whether a game can still be called “trivial”. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Silver et al., Nature, 2016 and 2017, and Science, 2018; NobelPrize.org (Chemistry 2024).

diapos.titre: Three victories, three ways to beat humans

evenements.texte: Calculation: 200 million positions per second and rules written by experts
Language: it wins *Jeopardy!*, a quiz full of wordplay, and 1 million dollars
Creativity: 10¹⁷⁰ positions in go; move 37 surprises its own makers
No human games: after 3 days of playing itself, it beats AlphaGo 100–0
From games to science: the shape of proteins, and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry

diapos.notes: A timeline to sum it all up. Three victories, three ways to beat humans, according to the NotebookLM decks: the power of calculation (Deep Blue, 1997), language and context (Watson, 2011), intuition, almost creativity (AlphaGo, 2016). Then two sequels: AlphaGo Zero does without humans (2017), and AlphaFold moves from games to science (Nobel Prize 2024). Notice the change of method: Deep Blue followed rules written by experts; AlphaGo learned from human games before playing against itself; AlphaGo Zero learns alone, from the rules. Historical detail: move 37 was played in the second game (the course places it in the third), and Lee Sedol only won the fourth. Tip: hide the years and ask the students to put the five events back in order, justifying it by the machine's method. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026) and the teacher's NotebookLM decks; IBM; DeepMind; NobelPrize.org.

diapos.texte: Until now, the machine judged. With the Transformer (2017), it learns to read whole texts, then starts to write, draw, compose and make videos.
diapos.notes: Remind the class of the road so far: the perceptron, the two winters, then the comeback of deep networks with AlexNet and AlphaGo. Until now, almost everything AI did came down to judging: cat or dog, the amount on a check, the risk of a disease. This seventh part tells the moment when the machine starts to produce. It follows four steps: the idea of generative AI; a Google paper published in 2017 that invents the Transformer; the race of the GPT models, up to ChatGPT in November 2022; and finally models that see, read and speak at once. It ends with the question the course has been asking from the start: after so many springs and winters, where do we stand in 2026? In less than ten years, we go from a research paper to tools that hundreds of millions of people use every week. Tip: ask for a show of hands: who used an assistant (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude…) this week, and for what? Write three uses on the board and come back to them on the last slide of the part. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); usage figures: OpenAI (2025–2026).

points: A photo: “cat or dog?”
A check: what amount is written?
A patient: what is the risk of disease?
It answers with a label or a percentage
It has learned patterns: faces, word order, sounds
It produces something new: images, music, stories
It imitates a style: “in the manner of Picasso, of Dalí”
Inventing a truly new style? The question is still open

diapos.notes: For a long time, AI sat exams: a photo, it answers “dog”; a check, it reads the figure; a patient's condition, it estimates the risk. An AI that sorts and predicts. Then researchers wonder: can a machine that has seen millions of cats draw one? That is generative AI: it no longer judges, it produces. It does not create from nothing: it has learned patterns (the shape of faces, the order of words, how sounds go together) and it recombines them. It takes the style, not the picture: at the end of March 2025, more than 130 million people made more than 700 million images in one week with ChatGPT, many “in the style of Studio Ghibli”. Yet in 2016 the studio's co-founder, Hayao Miyazaki, had called an AI-made animation “an insult to life itself”. In literature, this is called a *pastiche*; Arabic poetry has the *mu'arada* (Shawqi answering al-Busiri's *Burda*). Tip: have an assistant write a quatrain “in the manner of” a poet studied in class; the class decides: a good pastiche, or a creation? Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); OpenAI (April 2025); NHK, *Never-Ending Man: Hayao Miyazaki* (2016).

points: June 2017: eight Google researchers present the **Transformer**, tested on translation
It reads the whole sentence at once: **attention** links each word to those that explain it
“The student opened the book because she…”: “she” looks at “student”
It is the “T” in GPT; all large language models descend from it (part 9)
diapos.notes: 2017, says the course, is “the pivotal year”. Eight Google researchers publish a paper with a surprising title: *Attention Is All You Need*. It is a nod to the Beatles song *All You Need Is Love*, suggested by Llion Jones, one of the eight authors; the name “Transformer” was chosen by Jakob Uszkoreit, who liked the sound of it. The idea: instead of reading word after word, like a pupil following the line with a finger, the model looks at the whole sentence at once and asks, for each word, which other words give it its meaning. The Transformer was first tested on translation (from English into German and French), where it matched or beat the best systems. Today it is the T in GPT, *Generative Pre-trained Transformer*, and the 7th most cited paper of the 21st century according to *Nature*. Tip: write the sentence from the slide on the board and let the class draw an arrow to the word “she” looks at; go no further, the mechanism is opened in part 9. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Vaswani et al. (arXiv, June 2017); *Wired* (March 2024); *Nature* (April 2025).

evenements.texte: OpenAI trains GPT-1 on over 7,000 unpublished books; Google launches BERT
1.5 billion parameters; OpenAI delays its full release for fear of misuse
175 billion parameters: it drafts, summarizes and rephrases
November 30: 1 million users in 5 days, 100 million in 2 months
March 14: it also takes images and passes a simulated bar exam

diapos.notes: The course tells this race in a few sentences. GPT-1 (June 2018) was no genius, but it was the start of something very clever; it learned language from more than 7,000 unpublished books: adventure, fantasy, romance. In 2019, GPT-2 writes whole paragraphs: given the start of a fake news story about unicorns discovered in a valley in the Andes who speak perfect English, it invents the rest, down to the name of the species, “Ovid's Unicorn”. In 2020, GPT-3 drafts, summarizes, rephrases: poor by today's standards, but dazzling at the time. *The Guardian* even publishes an op-ed “written by a robot”: in fact, the editors assembled the best parts of eight texts produced by the machine. Then, on November 30, 2022, ChatGPT puts all this into a simple chat window. Tip: open the debate: who is the author of the *Guardian* op-ed? The machine, the person who wrote the prompt, or the editor who assembled the passages? Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); OpenAI papers and announcements (2018–2023); *The Guardian* (Sept. 8, 2020); UBS, via Reuters (Feb. 2023).

diapos.titre: Toward multimodal AI: seeing, reading, speaking

evenements.texte: A network that sees and a network that writes, stuck together, describe a photo
400 million image-text pairs: pictures and words in the same space
DALL·E 2, Stable Diffusion: an image is born from noise being removed
A large vision model is linked to a large language model
A single network for text, image and voice: about a third of a second to answer

diapos.notes: The word “multimodal” suggests a magic power; the NotebookLM decks show instead a chain of parts assembled step by step: first two separate systems, then a shared space (CLIP), then bridges between frozen models, finally models trained from the start on everything at once (GPT-4o, Gemini). Source: Ahmed El-Ghandour's course *The Last Invention* (2026) and the teacher's NotebookLM decks.

diapos.titre: 2026: eternal spring or a new winter?
points: AI has become multimodal: it writes, summarizes, draws, composes, makes videos, codes
The question of this whole history: do our expectations exceed its abilities?
If so, a new winter may come, even when the achievements remain huge
The lesson of the two winters: judge by results, not by promises
diapos.notes: Here we are in 2026. AI writes, summarizes, draws, composes music, makes videos with sound, codes, and often all of this in the same conversation. The course then asks the question that worries it most, the one we saw come back before every winter: have our expectations overtaken its abilities? A technology can be excellent, able to change the world, and still disappoint, because we expected far more from it. Remember the team that scored 5 goals: its next 2 goals felt like a failure. The signs point both ways. On the spring side: more than 900 million people use ChatGPT every week (OpenAI, February 2026). On the cloudy side: in 2025, the firm Gartner put generative AI in the “trough of disillusionment”; fewer than 30% of AI leaders say their CEO is happy with the return on investment. Nobody knows the future. Tip: draw the two curves on the board and ask three students to place 2026 on them: rising, peak, or falling expectations? Each one backs the answer with a fact, not a feeling. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); OpenAI (February 27, 2026); Gartner, *Hype Cycle for Artificial Intelligence* (August 2025).

diapos.texte: Let us open the machine: how does a network of artificial neurons learn? But first, a story.
diapos.notes: We have followed the history of AI up to today; we met the perceptron (1958) and backpropagation (1986). Now it is time to open the machine, as episode 3 of *The Last Invention* does. Here is the path of this part. First, a true and sad story: a car that “saw” without understanding. Then the idea of copying the brain. Then a guessing game that explains weights, bias and activation without any complicated formula. Finally, the three ways of learning, and the two mistakes of a machine that learns too much, or not enough. At the end we will come back to the car, and everyone will be able to explain what happened. Tip: first ask the class: “For you, what is learning: repeating, making mistakes, understanding?” Write the answers on the board; the machine will do the first two, but the third? Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).

points: 18 March 2018, about 10 p.m., Tempe (Arizona): a woman crosses a dark street with her bicycle
On the bicycle, her shopping bags. A car comes, does not brake in time: she dies
The car was driving itself: an Uber test, with a safety driver on board
Its sensors had “seen” her. Why did it not understand? Uber suspends its tests
diapos.notes: Tell it slowly, without drama. A Sunday evening, a wide, poorly lit avenue. A 49-year-old woman, Elaine Herzberg, is coming back from shopping: the bags hang on her bicycle, which she pushes by hand to cross the road, far from the crosswalk. Headlights appear. The car is doing over 60 km/h (nearly 40 mph) and does not brake in time. She dies shortly afterwards in hospital. At first we think of just another road accident: don't drive with your phone in your hand! Then comes the strange detail: the car was driving itself. Uber was testing its artificial intelligence; an employee sat behind the wheel to step in if needed, but she did not react in time. The recordings show that the car knew something was crossing in front of it. So why? The very next day, Uber suspends all its tests: first we must understand. Let us do the same. Tip: do not give the answer. Just ask: “If the car saw her, why did it not stop?” Keep the students' guesses on the board until the slide “Back to Tempe”. Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); NTSB report HAR-19/03 (2019).

points: To fly, we watched birds; to build intelligence, we watch the brain
The human brain has about 86 billion neurons, connected to each other
Understanding how they work may bring us closer to general AI
From this idea comes the artificial neural network: a very simplified copy
diapos.notes: How could we one day reach general AI? Episode 3 answers: by doing what humanity has always done, imitating nature. To fly, we watched birds. In 1900, Wilbur Wright described how he had watched buzzards: to keep their balance, they twist the tips of their wings. The Wright brothers turned this into the “wing warping” of their first machines. But a plane does not flap its wings: we copy the principle, not the feathers. For intelligence, the model is the human brain: about 86 billion neurons, according to a count published in 2009 (the round figure of “100 billion”, often repeated, had never been counted). An artificial neuron is a very simplified copy of a neuron: it receives signals, gives them more or less importance, and decides whether to pass something on. We have already met it with Rosenblatt's perceptron. Tip: ask the students for other inventions inspired by nature, then ask: is copying the shape of the brain the same as copying thought? Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Azevedo et al., *Journal of Comparative Neurology* (2009); Wilbur Wright, letter to Octave Chanute (1900).

diapos.titre: The guessing game: what is their job?
points: White coat, stethoscope around the neck: a doctor. Easy!
Now a team that knows nothing of our jobs; each member sees only one piece of the photo
One looks at the head (helmet? cap?), one at the clothes, one at the shoes
