Helmet 90%, vest 70%, safety boots 60%: the team concludes “engineer”
diapos.notes: Let us play, as in episode 3. First photo: a man all in white, a stethoscope around his neck. A doctor, easy. Now imagine a team from the Amazon rainforest: people who have never seen our modern jobs. And nobody sees the whole photo: I cut it up. The first one looks only at the head: helmet, cap or beret? The second at the clothes: coat, work overalls, jumpsuit? The third at the shoes: safety boots, army boots, sneakers? Each one reports. Head: “Something round, white, not very tall: 90% a helmet.” Clothes: “A small sleeveless garment, worn over the others, fluorescent color: 70% a vest.” Shoes: “Big shoes: 60% safety boots, 40% army boots.” I gather the reports and compare them with my list of jobs: it is an engineer. Nobody “understood” anything: we combined clues. Keep those 40% army boots in mind. Tip: have three volunteers act it out, each one seeing only a third of a printed photo. Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).

diapos.titre: Anatomy of a decision: weights, bias, activation
points: Weight = importance: helmet 100, vest 70, boots 50 (the most doubtful clue)
Bias: a number added to the sum that corrects a leaning (boots overrated)
Activation: not “engineer or not”, but “60% engineer, 30% soldier…”
diapos.notes: Not all information is equal: that is the weight, already seen with the perceptron. The helmet says a lot: weight 100. The vest a little less, because other jobs wear one too: 70. The boots left us unsure: 50. The course's formula: multiply each probability by its weight, add them up, then divide by the sum of the weights. 90 + 49 + 30 = 169, and 169 ÷ 220 ≈ 77%: engineer. (The video says 76%; the exact calculation gives 76.8%.) But this formula is linear: it can only separate cases with a straight line, like the perceptron facing the XOR wall. The course adds two settings. The bias: a number added to the sum that shifts the decision threshold and corrects a tendency, for example a team that gives the boots more importance than they deserve. The activation function: it breaks the straight line and gives a nuanced answer (60% engineer, 30% soldier, 10% something else) instead of a plain yes or no. Each designer chooses these functions according to what they want to get. Tip: do the calculation on the board with the class, calculators in hand. Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).

points: Same helmet, same vest, same boots… but camouflage clothes: a soldier on duty
The team answered “engineer”: the color of the clothes had no weight
We point out the mistake, it adjusts: from now on, color counts. That is learning
More teams (what he holds, what he rides, the setting) = more parameters = better answers
diapos.notes: On to level 2. I show my teams a new photo: helmet, vest, big boots. They do exactly the same work again and answer, full of confidence: “Engineer!” Wrong: it is a soldier on duty, in camouflage. Where is the mistake? Nobody had given any weight to the color of the clothes. So I go back to the teams: “Next time, give some weight to the color.” And so on, photo after photo: if the answer is right, well done; if it is wrong, we look for what was missing and change the weights. The team gets better with every mistake. To go further, I make the team bigger: one looks at what the man holds in his hand, another at what he rides (motorbike, tractor, car), another at the setting. A heap of sand and gravel behind an engineer? Our certainty can rise from 70% to 80%. More clues means more parameters, and more accurate answers. Tip: show another photo and ask the class which new clue should be added. Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).

diapos.titre: A neural network in one sentence
points: Each artificial neuron receives information and gives it a probability and a weight
It passes its conclusion on to the next layer, up to the final answer
Learning = adjusting the weights after each mistake: millions, then billions
All this without understanding anything: the founding idea of today's AI
diapos.notes: Here, in short, is what an artificial neural network is: our guessing teams. Each neuron looks at a small part of the problem. It gives what it sees a probability (am I sure it is a helmet?) and a weight (does this clue count a lot?), then passes its conclusion to the floor above. The course's example: a stethoscope around the neck weighs a lot for saying “doctor”; but is it really a stethoscope? That is the probability. Stack layers of these teams and you get a deep network. The number of these settings has exploded: remember the 175 billion parameters for GPT-3 in 2020, 671 billion for the Chinese model DeepSeek-V3 at the end of 2024. But learning is still the same thing: make a mistake, then adjust the weights. And none of these neurons “understands” what it does. Tip: ask three students to restate the idea in their own words, without using the word “neuron”. Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Brown et al., “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners” (2020); DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V3 technical report (2024).

points: Supervised: the teacher gives the right answer, even after a mistake (LeNet and the checks)
Unsupervised: “find on your own what repeats” (Google's cat, 2012)
Reinforcement: only “wrong” or “right”, never the answer (AlphaGo Zero, 2017)
ChatGPT uses all three: reading alone, imitating dialogues, then being rated by humans
diapos.notes: Our whole guessing game showed only one way of learning: supervised learning. The teacher knows the answer and gives it, even when the team got it wrong: “No, it is a soldier.” That is how LeNet learned to read the digits on checks, from thousands of labeled examples. Second way, unsupervised: we give the teams millions of images, videos and texts, and tell them: “Work it out yourselves, find what looks alike and what repeats.” In 2012, a Google network found the idea of “cat” on its own in 10 million images taken from YouTube. Third way, reinforcement: close to supervised learning, but the teacher never gives the solution. He only says “wrong, keep looking”, then “right!”. AlphaGo Zero (2017) learned Go this way, playing against itself, until it beat the version that had defeated Lee Sedol 100 to 0. As for ChatGPT, it read huge amounts of text, then imitated dialogues written by trainers, then humans ranked its answers. Tip: ask the students how they learned to swim, to read, to cook. Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Le et al. (2012); Silver et al., *Nature* (2017); OpenAI (2022).

diapos.titre: Learning too much, learning too little
points: Overfitting: in the training photos, every doctor wore glasses
The model gives glasses a weight of 100: a doctor without glasses? “Not a doctor”
Underfitting: the pupil who skims the book and misses important details
Same remedy: more data, more varied: day and night, places, colors, clothes
diapos.notes: Like a human, a network makes mistakes, in two opposite ways. Back to our game. Imagine that all the doctors in the training photos wore glasses. The model tells itself: “A doctor needs glasses to work, like a welder needs his mask.” It gives glasses a weight of 100. Along comes a doctor with a stethoscope, but no glasses: “Not a doctor!” That is overfitting: the model learned its examples by heart, accidental details included, instead of the rule. It is not just a fable: in 2016, researchers deliberately trained a model on photos in which every wolf stood in snow; it became… a snow detector. At the other extreme, underfitting: the pupil who skims the book and overlooks important details. The remedy is the same: more data, and more varied: by day and by night, old and new, other places, other colors, other clothes. Let the machine “see the world”. Tip: ask which accidental detail could fool an AI built to recognize the students of your faculty. Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Ribeiro, Singh and Guestrin, “Why Should I Trust You?” (2016).

points: Detected 5.6 s before impact, but labeled in turn vehicle, bicycle, “other”
The system did not expect pedestrians outside crosswalks (NTSB, 2019): too narrow a view
Emergency braking disabled in self-driving mode; the safety driver was looking at her phone
Uber's lesson, and ours: understand the machine before you trust it
diapos.notes: Let us go back to the dark street in Tempe: we now have the words to understand. In 2019 the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) established that the sensors had detected the pedestrian 5.6 seconds before impact. But the system never knew what it was seeing: vehicle, bicycle, “other object”? With each new label it recalculated her path, and it did not foresee that she would cross its own. Above all, its design did not take into account pedestrians crossing outside crosswalks. For this car, a human being walked on the white stripes: the course sees this as overfitting, too narrow a definition of a human. Just over a second before impact, the system worked out that emergency braking was needed, but that braking was disabled in self-driving mode: the safety driver was expected to act, and she was looking at her phone. In 2023 she pleaded guilty to endangerment. Tip: reread the guesses on the board, then open the debate: every year about 1.19 million people die on roads where humans drive; why do we demand more from a machine? Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); NTSB report HAR-19/03 (2019); WHO (2023).

diapos.titre: How does a machine read a text?
diapos.texte: We have seen how a model “sees”; it understands language in a fairly similar way. How does it turn words into numbers?
diapos.notes: Episode 3 ends with a promise. Remember the team from the Amazon: each member looked at one piece of the photo (the head, the clothes, the shoes), gave a probability, and the network weighed all these clues. That is how we understood how a machine can “see”. Ahmed El-Ghandour then adds: the way the model understands speech is not so different. A sentence, too, is cut into pieces; each piece becomes numbers; these numbers are weighed, compared and linked to one another. This part follows that path: from text to numbers (tokens), the map of meanings, the context that gives meaning (the attention of Transformers, 2017), then the machine that “writes” by guessing the next word. For literature students, this is the heart of the matter: the machine works on our raw material, language. Tip: ask for a show of hands: who thinks the machine reads letters, as we do? Ask again at the end of the part. Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026), which announces the next episode, on large language models.

points: A computer only knows numbers
The text is cut into pieces: **tokens**
Each token gets a number, then a long list of numbers: a **vector**
The model never sees letters, only these numbers
diapos.notes: The numbers in the picture are made up for the example. A real vocabulary has tens of thousands of tokens (just over 50,000 for GPT-2); a common word stays whole, a rare or long word is cut into several pieces. The colored columns stand for the vectors: hundreds of numbers per token, learned during training. Refer to the chapter 1 lesson “How an AI ‘understands’ a text”.

points: Each vector is an address on a huge map of meanings
Words with the same neighbors end up close: “cat”, “dog”
The model learns this by itself, guessing hidden words in billions of sentences
The map keeps relations: from “man” to “woman” as from “king” to “queen”
diapos.notes: A game to play with the class: “The ___ drinks milk and sleeps on the sofa.” Everyone guesses “cat” thanks to the neighbors: that is what the model does, on a huge scale. The linguist J. R. Firth put it this way in 1957: “You shall know a word by the company it keeps”. Real maps have hundreds of dimensions; here they are projected onto two. These maps also reproduce the stereotypes of their training texts.

points: The same word can have several meanings: “mouse”
**Attention** links each word to its neighbors
With “cheese”, the mouse is the animal; with “click”, it is the device
The word's vector is recalculated from its context
diapos.notes: This is what sets Transformers (2017) apart from older methods, which gave each word a single vector whatever its meaning. Other examples: “bank” (of a river, for money), “bat” (the animal, the stick). Ask the students for an example in another language: in Arabic, “عين” (the eye, a spring).

points: It splits the text into pieces, the tokens
It calculates the probability of each possible next token
It picks one, adds it to the text, and starts again
Humans then rate its answers to refine it
diapos.notes: It is the bigram model of notebook 08, on an immensely larger scale. Tuning by humans is called RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback. Stress this: the model predicts plausible text, not true text.

diapos.titre: A dialogue with a language model
diapos.legende: Fictional example, written for the class

echanges.texte: Explain forward chaining to a literature student.
Imagine a detective: he starts from the clues he knows and applies his rules one by one, until he finds the culprit.
Give me a reference so I can cite this in my thesis.
Careful: always check a reference in a library. I can make mistakes or invent references.

diapos.notes: Compare with ELIZA: this time, the answer is relevant, rephrased and adapted to its audience. But the risk remains: a model can invent a reference, a quotation, a date. This is the subject of the “reference test” activity in the guide.

diapos.texte: The language model no longer just answers: it plans, uses tools and acts.
diapos.notes: Final stage: this is what is in the news. Recall Shakey (1966): perceive, plan, act. The idea of an agent is old; what has changed is that a language model now serves as its “brain”.

points: An agent perceives its environment and acts on it to reach a goal
A thermostat is a very simple agent: it measures, then heats or not
Russell and Norvig (1995) define all of AI as the study of agents
A modern AI agent receives a goal, not just a question
diapos.notes: A definition for students to write down. The difference from a classic chatbot: we no longer ask it to “answer”, we ask it to “do”. Example: “Find three articles on Kateb Yacine, read them and write me a summary sheet.”

points: Goal: what the user asks for
Think: the model plans the next step
Act: it uses a tool (search, calculation, file, browser)
Observe: it reads the result, then starts again until the goal is reached
diapos.notes: Have students follow the animated loop. Each round can succeed or fail; the agent corrects its plan. That is why the tools it can access must be limited and its important actions checked.

diapos.texte: Eight centuries of dreams, seventy years of science, a few years of agents.
diapos.notes: Final part. At the start of episode 2, Ahmed El-Ghandour sums up the whole story in one sentence: AI starts small, almost trivial, then it grows, spreads and becomes immense. Check it with the class: the elephant clock described by al-Jazari in 1206; Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958), which learns to tell cards marked on the left from cards marked on the right; a network that reads the digits on bank checks in the 1990s; a program that beats one of the best Go players in the world (2016); then models that write and agents that act. Eight centuries of dreams, seventy years of science since Dartmouth (1956), a few years of agents. This part gathers the dates, the families of AI and the lessons, offers two videos, then checks with quizzes what has been understood. Tip: give each pair of students one of the ten previous parts; each pair sums it up in one sentence, then the class puts all the sentences back in order on the board. Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); al-Jazari, *The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices* (1206).

diapos.question: In what year did the term “artificial intelligence” take hold, with the Dartmouth workshop?
diapos.explication: The term appears in the 1955 proposal and took hold with the workshop in the summer of 1956.
diapos.notes: Have the class vote before revealing the answer (R key or button).

diapos.question: Why do we speak of AI “winters”?
choix: Disappointment made funding and interest fall
diapos.explication: After excessive promises, the results were disappointing: funding was cut (1974–1980, then 1987–1993).
diapos.notes: Ask for an example of an excessive promise seen in the lesson: Herbert Simon's quotation (1965).

diapos.question: What distinguishes an agent from a simple chatbot?
choix: It pursues a goal by acting with tools
diapos.explication: An agent chains actions (searching, calculating, writing a file…) and observes the results to reach a goal.
diapos.notes: Go back to the loop: goal, think, act, observe.

diapos.question: Did ELIZA (1966) understand what was said to it?
choix: No: it transformed sentences with rules
diapos.explication: ELIZA spotted keywords and sent back stock sentences. Believing that it understood is the “ELIZA effect”.
diapos.notes: A transition question to the debate: and do today's models understand?

diapos.question: Why can't the simple perceptron learn the “two-key door” (XOR)?
choix: It does not have enough memory
A single straight line does not separate the two groups
XOR does not exist in mathematics
It needs a more precise camera
diapos.explication: The perceptron draws a single straight border; XOR needs two rules on top of each other, so at least two layers, trained by backpropagation.
diapos.notes: Go back to the door image: open with one key, shut with zero or two keys.

diapos.question: A model has only seen doctors wearing glasses; faced with a doctor without glasses, it answers “not a doctor”. What is this flaw?
diapos.explication: It learned a detail of its examples by heart instead of the general rule: that is overfitting. Remedy: more numerous and more varied examples.
diapos.notes: Link the question to the Tempe accident (2018): a pedestrian outside the crosswalk did not look like the examples it had learned.

diapos.question: Google Translate is an example of which kind of AI?
diapos.explication: Brilliant at translation, it can neither play chess nor write code: it excels at a single task. That is narrow AI.
diapos.notes: Recall the image from episode 3. Google Translate has got you out of trouble more than once: it is a genius at translation. But this genius cannot play chess, or write a program, or do many things you do without effort. It is narrow AI, like Google Maps or the opponent in your video games: excellent in its field, lost outside it. General AI, which would move from one task to another like a human, remains theoretical; superintelligence remains an unknown. As for an agent, it is not defined by the range of its talents but by the way it acts: it pursues a goal with tools. Tip: have the class vote by show of hands before revealing the answer (R key), then ask each student for another example of narrow AI in their daily life (the keyboard that suggests the next word, the spam filter, unlocking a phone with your face). Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).

diapos.question: In 2012, what made AlexNet's victory possible?
choix: A brand-new algorithm, on its own
Millions of images, on their own
A deep network, ImageNet's images and graphics cards together
diapos.explication: The ideas dated from the 1980s; it also took ImageNet's images and the power of GPUs. The three gears finally met.
diapos.notes: Tell the scene from episode 2. In 2012, three researchers from Toronto, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and their professor Geoffrey Hinton, enter the ImageNet contest with a network trained not on the processor (CPU) but on two video-game graphics cards (GPUs). “One letter apart, years apart,” says Ahmed El-Ghandour. They do not just win: they crush the contest, with a 15.3% error rate against 26.2% for the runner-up. No single cause is enough. Backpropagation had existed since 1986; without ImageNet's 1.2 million training images, the network would have had nothing to learn from; without GPUs, which NVIDIA's CUDA (2007) made easy to program for general computing, a network with 60 million parameters was too heavy to train: with two cards, it took five to six days. It is the meeting of the three gears: algorithms, data, computing power. Tip: after the vote, ask: “If we remove just one gear, what happens?” Source: episode 2 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, *ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks*, NIPS, 2012.

diapos.question: Tempe, 2018: why did Uber's test car not react in time?
choix: It had no sensor able to see at night
It was driving far too fast to brake in time
It had not learned that people cross outside crosswalks, and hesitated over what it saw
The woman was invisible to its cameras and its radars
diapos.explication: Detected 5.6 s before impact, she was never recognized as a pedestrian: the system did not expect people to cross outside a crosswalk (NTSB, 2019).
diapos.notes: Go back to the night of March 18, 2018, in Tempe, Arizona, which opens episode 3. The three wrong answers are common misconceptions. The car had cameras, radars and a lidar; it was not over the speed limit; and it did “see” Elaine Herzberg, aged 49, 5.6 seconds before impact. But the system never classified her as a pedestrian: vehicle, bicycle, “other”? According to the NTSB investigation, it had not been designed for pedestrians crossing outside a crosswalk. For the car, a human was someone walking on the white stripes: Ahmed El-Ghandour sees this as a case of overfitting. Two human choices made things worse: automatic emergency braking was disabled in autonomous mode, and the safety driver was watching a video on her phone. Tip: ask who is responsible: the machine, the company or the driver? Link the answer to the question of part 1: who gave the machine power? Source: episode 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026); NTSB, report HAR-19/03 (2019).

points: AI has spread faster than the PC, mobile phone and Internet: states and jobs are at stake
AI imitates intelligence: it seems to understand; general AI does not exist yet
Rules and neurons take turns; winters are born of inflated expectations
2012: data, graphics cards and deep networks come together
A network weighs clues and corrects errors; it fails if it learns too much or too little
Who gives the machine power? Check, stay in control, declare your use
diapos.texte: Homework: choose a date from the timeline and write ten lines on what it changed, citing a verified source.
diapos.notes: At the start of this lesson, we promised to reveal the magician's trick. Here it is: the machine does not “understand” as we do; it cuts up, counts, weighs clues and corrects its errors, billions of times. Whether it reads a text or serves as an agent's “brain”, the principle is the same. That does not make it less impressive: we can better measure its skill, and we know where it can go wrong, as in Tempe. The six points follow the order of the lesson: why now, what AI is, its history and its winters, the breakthrough of 2012, the way a network learns, and the question that now matters: who gave the machine power, who tested it, who answers when it is wrong? Tip: bring out the questions the students wrote after “the magician's trick”: which ones have found an answer? Those still open will feed the round table on the origins of AI, which the homework prepares. Source: episodes 1 to 3 of *The Last Invention* (Ahmed El-Ghandour, 2026).
